title: Teaching at thirteen
hookLine: the young person reads Torah and teaches the community

lines: A VOICE CRACKS ON THE FIRST WORD.
cards: The voice cracks on the first word. Thirteen years old, standing at the reading table, a silver pointer in one hand, the open Torah scroll in front of them, a grandmother in the third row mouthing every syllable along.
The scroll has no vowels and no punctuation. They learned the melody for every word ahead of time, and now it's just them and the parchment. They get through it.
Then they turn around, unfold a piece of paper, and do something even more nerve-racking. They teach. The rabbi sits down and listens.

teach.b: First, going up. The young person is called to the Torah for an aliyah, a going up. They say the blessings before and after the reading, the same blessings any adult says, and often chant the reading itself.

Some also chant a portion from the Prophets, the haftarah. In some communities girls do this too; in Orthodox communities a girl often marks her bat mitzvah with a teaching at a meal or gathering instead.
It's called a d'var Torah, a word of Torah: a short talk on that week's portion. What puzzled me in it. What I think it means.
Why it matters now. The child who was licking honey off letters is now explaining the text to adults. Third, the command behind it.
Deuteronomy says: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children." For years, the community did exactly that.
Now the line turns around, and the child teaches back: not only a receiver of the tradition, but a new link, passing it on. Fourth, who learns.

teach.h: MOST OF ALL, FROM MY STUDENTS.
teach.b: The Talmud records a teacher who said he learned much from his teachers, more from his colleagues, and most of all from his students. And Pirkei Avot asks: who is wise? The one who learns from every person.
When a thirteen-year-old teaches, the adults in the room get the chance to be that kind of wise.

how: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person is often called up to the Torah, chants the reading or the haftarah, and gives a d'var Torah, a short teaching on the week's portion, to the congregation.

practice: Choose one thing you've learned, on this path or anywhere, that you could explain in a minute: a word, a custom, a story, a way of fixing a bike.
Shape it the way a d'var Torah goes, what puzzled me, what I think it means, why it matters now, three sentences said inside. Then think of one person who might want to hear it.
